quiz_title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th Edition) - Top 10 Questions

questions.question_text: According to the AIMA fourth edition, what is referred to as the 'Standard Model' of AI?

options.A: Programs that can pass the Turing Test.
options.B: The modeling of human brain function using neural networks.
options.C: The study and construction of rational agents that do the 'right thing,' as defined by a provided objective.
options.D: Systems that accurately mimic human thinking processes.

questions.explanation: On page 22, the text states: 'In a nutshell, AI has focused on the study and construction of agents that do the right thing. What counts as the right thing is defined by the objective that we provide to the agent. ... we might call it the standard model.'

questions.question_text: What is the primary issue described by the authors as the 'Value Alignment Problem'?

options.A: The slow processing speed of AI systems.
options.B: The gap between the true preferences of humans and the objectives we put into the machine.
options.C: AI systems make too many mathematical calculation errors.
options.D: The lack of sufficient data for machine learning.

questions.explanation: On page 23, it is explicitly stated: 'The problem of achieving agreement between our true preferences and the objective we put into the machine is called the value alignment problem.'

questions.question_text: In AI, what is the formal definition of an 'Agent'?

options.A: A robot that mimics human actions.
options.B: A program that automatically searches the internet.
options.C: A piece of software that executes a predefined program.
options.D: Anything that can perceive its environment through sensors and act upon that environment through actuators.

questions.explanation: On page 54, the definition is given: 'An agent is anything that can be viewed as perceiving its environment through sensors and acting upon that environment through actuators.'

questions.question_text: What is the definition of a 'Rational Agent'?

options.A: An agent that selects an action expected to maximize its performance measure, given the evidence and its built-in knowledge.
options.B: An agent that always knows the best possible outcome.
options.C: An agent that makes perfect, error-free decisions.
options.D: An agent that accurately mimics human decision-making.

questions.explanation: On page 58, the definition is: 'For each possible percept sequence, a rational agent should select an action that is expected to maximize its performance measure, given the evidence provided by the percept sequence and whatever built-in knowledge the agent has.'

questions.question_text: What does the acronym PEAS describe for an agent?

options.B: The complexity level of an algorithm.
options.C: The programming standards for writing code.

questions.explanation: On page 60, it is stated: 'We group all these under the heading of the task environment. For the acronycally minded, we call this the PEAS (Performance, Environment, Actuators, Sensors) description.'

questions.question_text: Which of the following environment types is described as the hardest for agent design?

options.B: Partially observable, multiagent, nondeterministic, sequential, dynamic, continuous, and unknown.
options.D: Fully observable, multiagent, sequential, dynamic, continuous.

questions.explanation: On page 64, the text says: 'The hardest case is partially observable, multiagent, nondeterministic, sequential, dynamic, continuous, and unknown.' It then gives taxi driving as an example.

questions.question_text: Which type of agent maintains an internal state, using both a transition model and a sensor model?
questions.explanation: On page 70, the text states: 'An agent that uses such models is called a model-based agent.'

questions.question_text: What is the primary disadvantage of Breadth-first search?

options.A: It is not suitable for dynamic environments.
options.B: It cannot find the optimal solution.
options.C: It is an incomplete search algorithm.
options.D: Its memory requirements grow exponentially with depth.

questions.explanation: On page 95, the text explains: 'All the nodes remain in memory, so both time and space complexity are O(b^d). ... The memory requirements are a bigger problem for breadth-first search than the execution time.'

questions.question_text: Which algorithm should be used to find a cost-optimal solution when actions have different costs?
questions.explanation: On page 95, the text states: 'When actions have different costs, an obvious choice is to use best-first search where the evaluation function is the cost of the path ... This is called ... uniform-cost search.' It is complete and optimal.

questions.question_text: For A* search to guarantee cost-optimality, the heuristic function h(n) must have which property?

options.B: It must be admissible (never overestimates the cost to reach the goal).

questions.explanation: On page 104, the text clearly states: 'A key property is admissibility: an admissible heuristic is one that never overestimates the cost to reach a goal. ... With an admissible heuristic, A* is cost-optimal.'
